name: Flattop

lead: A flattop is a classic men's cut with short back and sides and a top that is cut flat and stands upright. The squared silhouette adds height at the crown and an angular, structured look to the head.
It was popular in the early and mid 20th century, associated with athletes, soldiers and astronauts, and still has dedicated wearers.

paras: Barbers do most of the work with clippers, using clipper-over-comb and freehand techniques on the top, then finish with shears. Wax, pomade, gel or hairspray help the top stand up.
No health risks. The shape grows out quickly, and wearers typically book cuts every two to three weeks. It needs enough hair density on top to stand up.

chain: Flat top cut over short tapered sides
Angular, structured head and jaw look
angle.text: The flat upright top adds apparent height and a geometric outline, which people choose to make the head look more angular and the jaw more prominent.

lead: A flattop is a hairstyle with short sides and back and a top cut short, upright and level so that it forms a flat surface. It is a classic men's cut that was popular in the early and mid twentieth century and still has dedicated wearers.[1]

For appearance, the flat plane adds height at the top of the head and a squared, geometric outline that emphasises the angles of the jaw and head shape. People choose it for the structured silhouette, and for a cut that stays tidy with little daily styling beyond a firm product.[1][2] Variants include the classic, a counterculture version with a longer top, the flattop with fenders, and the horseshoe flattop.[1]

The cut belongs to the crew-cut family, in which the top is graduated in length and, when it forms a level or sloping plane, is called a flat top. Wikipedia groups the crew cut, flat top, butch and Ivy League cuts together as types of buzz cut, and records that the flat top was the most popular version of the crew cut in the 1980s.[3][4] Mid-century publications such as Life (1956) and Time (1959) covered it, and butch wax was the product name tied to it in the 1950s.[1]
infobox: About 1/4 inch at crown, 3/4 to 1 1/4 inch front[1]
Cut every two to three weeks[1]
Crew cut, brush cut, butch, high and tight[3][5]

paras: The classic version is cut flat from front to back and rounded at the crown, with the top about a quarter inch at the highest point of the crown and three-quarters to one and a quarter inches toward the front, and the back and sides around a quarter inch and tapered into the top. Ears are cleanly outlined, sideburns squared just above the ear opening and the neckline given a low taper.[1]

The counterculture variant leaves the top two or three inches in front, with the back and sides left long or shaved. The flattop with fenders slicks long sides back into a ducktail. The horseshoe flattop shaves the back and sides to the skin from the crown's highest back point, leaving a horseshoe-shaped area of hair on top, a version Wikipedia says soldiers in the US military often wore.[1] Some versions show a strip of scalp at the center top, called a landing strip, after an aircraft carrier's flight deck; wearers often discuss whether they want one.[1] The related high-and-tight is a military variant of the crew cut with very closely clipped sides and a top of roughly 5 to 10 mm, which spread into civilian use from the late 1980s according to Wikipedia.[5]

Skull shape, hair density and shaft thickness limit the options. Thick, upright hair holds the flat plane most easily, and Wikipedia's crew-cut article says a well-suited head shape can make the cut work with finer hair.[1][3]

Wikipedia's crew-cut article traces the underlying short cut, known earlier as the short pompadour or brush cut, to at least the mid-eighteenth century, and says the 'crew cut' name most likely comes from university rowing crews at Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Cornell. Before motorised electric clippers appeared in 1921, barbers regarded the perfect short pompadour as one of the most time-consuming styles to trim.[3]

The crew cut was popular among college students in the 1920s and 1930s, spread widely through military haircuts during World War II, declined from the mid-1960s as long hair became fashionable, and returned in the late 1970s and early 1980s.[3] Wikipedia's flattop page dates photographs of flattop wearers from about 1906 and cites barbering textbooks by Thorpe (1967) and Trusty (1971).[1] A 1956 Life article, 'How To Square Flattop Hair', and a 1959 Time piece on teenage fashions are cited as period coverage.[1]

Grokipedia's AI-generated account adds that the 1950s boom included Ivy League and greaser subcultures using pomade, that punk, skinhead, psychobilly and rockabilly scenes revived it in the 1980s, and that in the 1990s hip-hop fused it with the high-top fade; its own sourcing is described as uneven, so these details are best read as that page's claims.[2]

sections.h: How it is cut and kept
paras: Clippers do most of the work. The lower sides and back are cut with a quarter-inch or shorter guard or detachable blade, the upper sides are boxed in rather than contoured using clipper-over-comb, and the top is usually cut with clipper-over-comb, though shears-over-comb or freehand clipper work is also used. Some barbers use a wide four-inch comb or wide rotary clipper blades, and master barbers finish with shears in a move called the scissor salute.[1]

Products named include wax pomade, hairspray, mousse, gel and cream, chosen by hair texture and by how stiff or shiny the wearer wants the result; coarse hair may hold with little product, but most wearers use a blow dryer.[1] Because the shape grows out quickly, maintenance cuts are needed every two to three weeks, and some wearers go weekly, a habit barbers call Flattop Friday.[1]

Wikipedia's captions name Johnny Unitas, Gary Thompson, Chris Mullin and Howie Long from sport, astronauts Walter Cunningham and Doug Hurley, flight director Gene Kranz, politicians H.R. Haldeman and Jon Tester, and historical figures including Pierre Curie, Paul von Hindenburg and Karel Kramar.[1]

Grokipedia describes the cut as signalling discipline and conformity in military, police and conservative professional settings, and as signalling rebellion in rockabilly, punk and hip-hop contexts, with online barber tutorials and TikTok barber challenges credited for renewed interest among younger people.[2]

Grokipedia says the cut often produces a squarish or rectangular silhouette that can enhance facial structure, that rounder heads may call for adjustments, and that fine hair may need styling aids to look fuller.[2] Wikipedia's buzz-cut article says very short cuts can make the face look more defined.[4]

timeline.event: Yale's championship football team appears with close-cropped hair, a moment Wikipedia's crew-cut article cites in the shift away from long hair in football.[3]
Motorised electric clippers appear, easing the short pompadour and crew-cut family of cuts for barbers.[3]
Crew cuts become popular among US college students, especially in the Ivy League.[3]
World War II drafts give many men a G.I. crew cut, and many keep it as civilians.[3]
Life publishes a piece on how to square flattop hair.[1]
Short cuts decline as long hair becomes fashionable.[3]
The flat top is the most popular version of the crew cut.[3]
